records.name: Guam
records.summary:
An unincorporated US territory, so the 2025–26 federal turn — marker/document policy, TSA screening, the trans military-exclusion order — lands hard on an island whose economy and society carry a large permanent US military presence. Local law partly cuts the other way: Guam was the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage (2015, after a local lesbian couple sued over a denied licence), its statute book bars employment discrimination including gender identity, and federal hate-crime coverage has applied since 2009.

Academic Pacific-identity surveys record indigenous Chamorro understandings of gender diversity, and a local advocacy scene maintains ID-documents guidance for residents. The synthesis for a visitor: real written protections and a quiet, integrated public record, against military-community conservatism, federal volatility amplified by the base, and small-island visibility where an outed stranger is noticed.

sources.summary: A4TE 'Know Your Rights: Airport Security': TSA body-scanner and pat-down procedures can 'out' trans travellers; the guide covers pre-flight packing, document/screening mismatches, the right to request alternative screening, and how to escalate airport problems. Notes most trans travellers pass screening without incident. In scope for Guam as a US-territory TSA jurisdiction — visitor-facing screening guidance.

NPR (28 Jan 2025): Trump executive order bans transgender troops from serving openly; SecDef Hegseth given 30 days to submit an implementation plan; the order frames trans identity as 'radical gender ideology'. US-national military policy applying in Guam given the large permanent US military presence recorded on the record.

Guardian/AP (5 Jun 2015): chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's same-sex marriage prohibition after an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero denied a licence; ruling effective 8am Tuesday 9 June — Guam became the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

records.name: U.S. Virgin Islands
records.summary:
A small US territory: federal document and airport policy applies, and the 2025–26 federal turn is felt through it (marker disputes, screening friction) with no local statute to soften it. Locally the record is quietly protective rather than hostile: the Attorney General ruled in 2017 that the human-rights law's sex provision covers transgender students — an official extension of territorial protection — and local media framed the community's position after the 2016 federal shock as 'losses... but reason for hope.'

No criminalisation, documented anti-trans enforcement or care ban appears in the audited record; equally, protection rests on an attorney-general's interpretation rather than legislation, and the islands' scale (tens of thousands across three main islands) means high everyday recognition risk. Federal rollback above, a thin but genuinely welcoming local posture beneath.

sources.summary: A4TE airport guide, applicable to USVI travellers as US nationals: TSA body-scanner flags and pat-downs, documentation mismatches, requesting alternative screening; plus carry-on/prohibited-items advice -- the federal screening framework USVI residents and visitors stand under.
St. John Source (March 2017): the Attorney General ruled the USVI anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students - official interpretation extending territorial protections.
St. Thomas Source (July 2017): 'LGBTQ community see losses in territory but reason for hope' - local reporting on the community's setbacks and prospects in the USVI.

Overview: discrimination protections on sexual-orientation (and gender-identity) grounds in the territory's human-rights law; same-sex marriage legal since a 2015 territorial court ruling found denial unconstitutional; historic sodomy statute (1957 application) superseded -- rights baseline for the USVI (fetched, article text verified).

Overview: a 2015 territorial Superior Court ruling struck down the denial of marriage licences to same-sex couples, legalising same-sex marriage in the USVI; later federal recognition settled nationwide -- marriage status visitors can rely on (fetched, article text verified).
